title: Tisha B'Av: Lamentations
hook: read by candlelight, sitting low; the Talmud says the second Temple fell for baseless hatred (Yoma 9b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bein hametzarim, the fast that opens three weeks of mourning. Your line was walls breached. Did you find a crack that needs mending? Three weeks later, the fire. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Evening, in a synagogue, on the ninth of Av. The big lights are off or turned low. In many places the curtain has been taken down from the ark. People have come in sneakers or cloth shoes, because leather is set aside for the day. Nobody greets anyone. They don't sit on the benches; they sit on the floor, or on low stools, the way mourners sit at home. Someone has a candle, someone has a phone flashlight. And then a reader begins a slow, falling chant, and the first word is a cry.
screen: `THE LIGHTS GO LOW.` → `NO LEATHER, NO GREETINGS.` → `EVERYONE SITS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: The word is eicha. It means how, the kind of how you say when you can't believe what you're seeing. It's the first word of the book of Lamentations, and Jews call the whole book by it. The old Jewish translation opens: How doth the city sit solitary. Jerusalem, once full of people, sits alone like a widow. The book has five chapters, and four of them are built on the alphabet, verse by verse, from the first letter to the last, as if grief needed every letter there is. Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the day the tradition remembers both Temples falling: the first to Babylon, the second to Rome, centuries apart, mourned on one day. It's a full fast, from sunset to the next nightfall. Now the question every mourner asks: why? The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, gives an answer that has stung for centuries. The first Temple, it says, fell because of idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed. But the second Temple? People then studied Torah, kept the commandments, and did acts of kindness. So why did it fall? Because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred. Hatred for nothing, for no reason worth the name. And the Talmud adds that baseless hatred weighs as much as those three great sins together. Notice what that does. The rabbis didn't only blame the empire with the battering rams. They looked at their own community: the feuds, the contempt, the neighbor nobody would speak to. And the book doesn't end in the dark. Its last chapter asks God to turn us back and renew our days as of old, and because the very last verse is so bitter, the congregation goes back and says that line again.
screen: `EICHA: HOW?` · `TWO TEMPLES, ONE DAY OF MOURNING.` · `NOT ONLY ROME: BASELESS HATRED.` · `SAY THE HOPEFUL LINE AGAIN.` · then, large: `BASELESS HATRED DESTROYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one grudge. If you can, sit low, on the floor or on a step. Let your breathing settle. Then let one grudge come to mind, the kind that isn't about anything big anymore: an old slight, a sibling's tone, a neighbor you decided long ago not to like. Look at what it's built on. Often, not much. You don't have to forgive the unforgivable, and you don't have to call anyone. Just, for this minute, set this one down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor. Notice your shoulders when it's gone. The bell holds the time.
Eicha. How: the first word and the Hebrew name of Lamentations, read on Tisha B'Av, sitting low. Today's word.
Your line: baseless hatred destroys. Today, catch one moment of contempt, in your head, online or out loud, and let it go unsaid. Day six hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations chanted in a dim synagogue, followed by kinot, poems of mourning.

Yoma 9b says they studied, kept the commandments and did kindness; it fell for baseless hatred.

fork.setup: you're a sage after the second Temple burned. the people studied and kept the commandments. why did it fall?
fork.reveal: the Talmud (Yoma 9b) says baseless hatred, and that it weighs as much as idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed together.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old book of sad poems.
what it means: eicha, how: Lamentations, read on Tisha B'Av for both Temples.
what a scholar hears: four acrostic chapters, the third with three verses per letter; Yoma 9b turns the blame inward, to sinat chinam.

sources.quoted: How doth the city sit solitary

notes: Quoted Lamentations 1:1 opening phrase as in JPS 1917 ('How doth the city sit solitary'); verify capitalization and wording.
Yoma 9b paraphrased: first Temple for idolatry, forbidden relations, bloodshed; second for sinat chinam, which is equal to the three. Verify.
Customs (no leather shoes, sitting on floor/low stools, no greetings, dimmed lights, removing the parochet in some communities) vary; check phrasing.
Chapters 1, 2, 4 are single acrostics; chapter 3 is a triple acrostic; chapter 5 is not an acrostic. Some chapters reverse ayin and pe.
Repeating 5:21 after 5:22 so the reading ends on hope: a widespread custom; verify.
Tisha B'Av runs about 25 hours, sunset to the following nightfall.
